title: Consistent hashing
summary: Why hash mod N reshuffles almost every key when a node joins, how a ring with virtual nodes moves only about 1/(N+1) of them, and rendezvous hashing as the simpler alternative.

steps.title: The trouble with mod N
body: `shard = hash(key) mod N` spreads keys evenly. Now add one node. Almost every key's `mod` changes, so almost
every key moves. For a cache tier that means almost every lookup misses at once and the database takes the
whole load. For a database it means copying nearly all the data.
Step through 12 keys going from 3 nodes to 4. Only keys 0, 1 and 2 stay put.
> **Rule of thumb:** going from N to N+1 nodes with mod N, only about **1 in N+1** keys stays where it was.

steps.prompt: Twenty keys, going from 4 nodes to 5 with mod N. What does this print?
steps.explain: `k % 4 == k % 5` only for k = 0 to 3 in every block of 20 (the lcm of 4 and 5). So 4 stay and 16 of 20 move: 80%.

steps.title: The ring
body: **Consistent hashing** puts nodes and keys on the same circle of hash values (say 0 to 2^32 - 1). A key belongs
to the first node **clockwise** from it. Add node D and it only takes the keys between its predecessor and
itself; every other key stays where it was.
```text
D(55)  <- new: takes k45, k50 from C
The trace below uses a tiny ring of 0 to 99. Watch which keys change owner when D joins at 55. With N nodes,
a new one takes about **1/(N+1)** of the keys, all of them from one neighbour (with virtual nodes, from many).

steps.explain: No node sits clockwise between 72 and the top of the ring, so the key wraps around to the first node, A at 10.

steps.title: Virtual nodes, and rendezvous hashing
body: Three points on a ring make very uneven arcs: one node might own half the circle. And when a node dies, its
whole arc lands on **one** neighbour, which may then fall over too.
**Virtual nodes** fix both: each physical node is placed at many points (`A#0`, `A#1`, ... `A#99`). Arcs average
out, so load is even, and a dead node's keys spread over all the survivors. Stronger machines get more points.
| Technique | Lookup | Moves when a node joins | Notes |
| `hash mod N` | O(1) | about N/(N+1) of keys | fine when N never changes |
| Ring + virtual nodes | O(log V) binary search | about 1/(N+1) | Cassandra-style tokens, many client libraries |
| **Rendezvous** (highest random weight) | O(N): score every node, pick the max | about 1/(N+1) | no ring to store; simple and even |
| Jump consistent hash | O(log N), no memory | about 1/(N+1) | nodes must be numbered 0..N-1; only add or remove the last |
Rendezvous: for each node compute `hash(node + key)` and pick the node with the highest score. Remove a node
and only the keys it won move, each to its runner-up.
- **Virtual node**: one of many points a physical node takes on the hash ring, so arcs and failover load are even.

steps.prompt: A cache tier has 4 nodes. You add a 5th. Roughly what share of keys move with `hash mod N`, and with a ring with virtual nodes?
options: About 80% with mod N, about 20% with the ring
About 25% with mod N, about 5% with the ring
steps.explain: With mod N only 1 in N+1 = 1 in 5 keys stays (20%), so 80% move. A ring moves only the share the new node should own: about 1/5.

prompt: **Symptom first.** At 14:10 an engineer removed one unhealthy node from a 10-node memcached tier. Clients
pick a node with `hash(key) % servers.Count`. Within a minute the cache hit rate fell from 96% to 11% and the
database's read QPS went up eight times. What happened?
options: Changing the node count from 10 to 9 remapped about 90% of the keys, so almost every read missed and went to the database
The removed node held all the hot keys
memcached flushes every node when one leaves
The database got slower, which lowered the hit rate
steps.explain: With mod N almost every key changes node, so the warm cache is useless until it refills. A consistent-hashing client (a ring such as ketama, or rendezvous) would have moved only the removed node's tenth of the keys.

steps.title: A hash ring with virtual nodes
prompt: - `HashRing(int vnodes)`: how many points each node gets.
- `void Add(string node)`: put the node on the ring at `H.Hash($"{node}#{i}")` for `i` from `0` to `vnodes - 1`.
- `void Remove(string node)`: take all its points off.
- `string NodeFor(string key)`: the owner of the first point whose position is **greater than or equal to**
`H.Hash(key)`, wrapping round to the first point. Throw `InvalidOperationException` when the ring is empty.
`H.Hash(string)` is given (a stable 32-bit hash returning `uint`); do not write it. Keep the points in a sorted
`List<uint>` and use `BinarySearch`: a negative result `i` means "insert at `~i`".
The tests put 3,000 keys on A, B and C, check the load is even, add D and check that keys only move **to** D,
then remove D and check every key is back.
solution: foreach (var p in owner.Where(kv => kv.Value == node).Select(kv => kv.Key).ToList())
if (points.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("the ring is empty");
hints: Keep two things: a sorted `List<uint>` of positions and a `Dictionary<uint, string>` from position to node.
`points.BinarySearch(h)` returns the index if found, else the complement of where it would go: `if (i < 0) i = ~i;`.
If `i == points.Count` the key is past the last point: wrap to index 0.

Dojo.Check("every key lands on A, B or C", dojoBefore.Values.All(n => n is "A" or "B" or "C"), "NodeFor returned something else");
Dojo.Eq("the same key always lands on the same node", dojoBefore["user:42"], dojoRing.NodeFor("user:42"));
var dojoShares = dojoBefore.Values.GroupBy(n => n).ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count() / 3000.0);

Dojo.Check("100 virtual nodes keep the load even (each node 20% to 46%)", dojoShares.Count == 3 && dojoShares.Values.All(s => s > 0.20 && s < 0.46), string.Join(", ", dojoShares.Select(kv => $"{kv.Key} {kv.Value:P0}")));
Dojo.Check("adding D moves keys only to D", dojoMoved.All(k => dojoRing.NodeFor(k) == "D"), "a key moved between two old nodes");
